utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. We have before the Trial Chamber this morning a couple of motions which have been filed for some time. Mainly because we hadn't received the reactions to them, we did not bring them up for arguments. But now we have received reactions in respect of a few of them. There is one we can hear without any formal reaction, a reply from the Prosecution. I think we can deal with that first before we consider the other motions. Now, we have Zdravko Mucic's confidential motion for protective measures in respect of witnesses DA2, DD2, DC2, DE2, DF2 and DG2 filed on the 5th of June. Is Mr. Mucic's Counsel prepared to argue it now?

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Yes, we are, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Has the Prosecution any views on the confidential motion? If you have, then we'll know what to do with this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, Teresa McHenry for the Prosecution. The Prosecution would defer to the Court about the motion for protective orders. I just would note, I assume Defence Counsel is aware that with respect to some witnesses, depending on the nature of their testimony, and the exact nature of their relationship, it may be that some of them are going to, in effect, have to testify in private session. In other words, it's possible that their testimony will, in effect, reveal their identity. But I assume that's something that Defence Counsel is aware of one way or the other. I just note that as an issue that occurred to us. But with respect to the merits of the motion, we defer to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. We pretty much outlined all our reasons, the argument in the motion before you, and so we also defer the matter to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think the main consideration is in nature of the protection that you actually require, because that should be consistent with the nature of the testimony of the witness, and the circumstances in which he finds himself in The Hague. Why are there are so many of them, from A to D, to K, isn't it? The relief you require, this is what I --

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: You see, Your Honours, all these witnesses are very close members of the family, actually the family itself, and some very close friends. As you very well know, the war may have ended in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but it has left very deep scars, tensions still run very high, and the healing process is a very slow one. These people have to return to their homeland and live with other ethnic groups. And for all these reasons, both personal and both subjective ones, we don't think that the grounds are -- all these reasons are fairly grounded, you know, for the motion to be accepted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: How do you justify your protection in respect of D -- A, B, C, D?

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Well, for all these reasons, especially Witness D, because Witness D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Not Witness D. Reason D.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Oh, reason D.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Relief D.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Well, we justify it because, Your Honours, although we are calling all these witnesses, there may be a situation that we might not put all -- you know, the particular -- one particular witness on the stand. Then we would, of course, notify the Chambers of our decision. And especially if some of these witnesses express their wish that they not be protected, and of course we'll notify the Trial Chamber and then we'll ask for the cessation for these measures to apply. But for the time being they have all expressed the wish to be protected. So that's what we are passing onto the Chambers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Will you be satisfied if the names are not disclosed to the public and the faces are not shown to the public, these two measures only? Will you be satisfied with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Definitely would be satisfied. But we would most certainly ask, you know, for all these measures --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am just asking you. This is what privilege has been granted to the Prosecution witnesses. Will you be satisfied with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Definitely, we will be satisfied. With these witnesses, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The interest is that the identity of the witness not be disclosed, so that any other device which enable you to maintain their position should be sufficient?

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: I think it would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You will be satisfied with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: We will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Names not disclosed, face not --

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Image distorted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: To that extent, I think we can grant this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: In respect of that protection, I think this would be sufficient for you, and the Trial Chamber will grant that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: But otherwise the presence in the witness box and they will be known by the accused persons, will see them, and Counsel will see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Now, the next motion we have is the motion by the defendant, Delalic, requesting procedures of final determination of the charges against him. The Prosecution has reacted to that in reply. Is Counsel prepared to argue that?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know whether this a mistake. We have not received their reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The Prosecution replied yesterday to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I haven't got it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have not received this reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I haven't too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We'll have to wait until you receive the reply. We have other motions by Hazim Delic. Do you remember when last it was raised and was argued already on the 28th of May. Ms. McHenry, what was the motion you replied to?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Excuse me. Your Honours, on the 2nd of June the Defence of Mr. Delalic filed a motion regarding the presentation of evidence. We responded to that yesterday. It is unfortunately entitled "Prosecution motion to exclude presentation of evidence immediately after the close of Delalic Defence." I think it would have been more appropriately entitled "Prosecution opposition to Defence motion" to do this. But it is, in effect, a response to the Defence motion. And I think it would be more expeditiously considered by the Chamber as a response rather than as a new motion. We apologise. As Your Honours know, their motion was filed very quickly, and rather than wait until the 14 days, when Your Honours indicated yesterday that you wanted to hear it, we very quickly prepared a response. And so I think we did not entitle it in the best possible way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It's not an independent motion, yours, it's a reply?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That's why in most cases it's better to reply in the title to which the motion was made.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You are absolutely right, Your Honour. I actually think we did the same thing with respect to expert witnesses in the recent past, and that is also, I think, not the best way to reply. And we will try to be paying more attention to that, despite even when we are replying very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I was referring to Delic's motions, which was partly considered, but not concluded, because of certain shortcomings in the motion itself. Where do you stand now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: We actually submitted two motions, Your Honours. One of them refers to the issuance of a binding order for the production of documents, a binding order on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. As the Prosecutor objected, saying that we did not, prior to that, address the Government of the Federal Republic, the liberation of this particular motion was postponed. We did address the Government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia through its Embassy in The Hague, but to this date we have received no reply from them. Perhaps we should wait for a couple days more and then the Defence will adopt a final position as to whether it will continue to seek the issuance of this binding order for the production of documents of evidentiary documents. Since some 11 or 12 days have elapsed since then, and in view of the fact that this involves contacts between organs which are here in Holland and those in Belgrade, we believe that perhaps we should wait for a while more and then the Defence will finally decide whether it will seek this motion, continue to seek this motion, or will be satisfied otherwise, and give it up as a matter of fact. The second motion that we filed was the one which we requested an expert opinion to be given by -- I cannot recall the name of the gentleman at this particular moment, but it was a police inspector who was to prove the consequences which emanate from a man being hit with a baseball bat, from his experience. As regards to that particular motion, the Trial Chamber instructed us that we were to submit a request for that fact to be elucidated, for that fact to be ascertained by a specialist doctor, a forensic medical expert. I am in touch with my colleague in Houston, and so far we have not found the suitable person to do that, and we will be doing that subsequently, after we have found the one. So we propose that the consideration of both motions of ours be postponed for a later date. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I'm not too sure from your motion whether your request to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, even if it is true, the Embassy here was made, because normally at least that should have been an annexe to your motion indicating the documents you are asking for. So that if there is any discussion, one has to exercise it, it will be based on their action that that has been done, and not for some time you've not had any reaction from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. You did not even say any such thing?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. We sent the request to Yugoslavia on the same date when the Trial Chamber was deciding this motion, and objected, because we had not, prior to submitting the motion to the Chamber, had not contacted the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. So that is why it was not discussed. But on that same day we submitted our request to the Embassy of Yugoslavia here in The Hague and in it we asked for all those documents which are enumerated in our submission. So far we have had no reaction on the part of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. What we do have is confirmation that it has been received by the Embassy and conveyed to its proper destination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we'll expect to hear later on that. Now, we have also some motions from Esad Landzo, a request for leave to call expert witnesses, two additional expert witnesses. I think the Prosecution has reacted to that and I would like to hear Counsel on that motion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Cynthia McMurrey and Nancy Boler for Esad Landzo. There's been so many back and forth motions with the Prosecution regarding the designation of experts. I believe that Ms. McHenry and I had a conversation this morning and we are clear as to which experts it is that need to be designated and which don't. I do have some news for the court today. I believe the Prosecution's response regarding Dr. Edward Gripon, has mostly been that they object to the fact that he has not presented a report and he has not completed his evaluation. He arrived in The Hague last night, he is in the courtroom today, and he will be completing his evaluation in the next few days. But just for verification, and if the Prosecutor would like, I can certainly call Mr. Gripon right now into the courtroom, let him swear under oath. Because they have called him on the telephone and they represented that he told them that he could have his report in five days. There was an affidavit attached to that response that I filed saying that Dr. Gripon said, when requested to write a report, he could have the report within five days. I have not requested him to write a report at this time, because he has not completed his evaluation. He will be here in The Hague until Friday to complete his evaluation, and after that time, if Defence Counsel requests a report, he will write a report, and I will most certainly disclose to the Prosecution. As of today, every expert report that I have in my possession has been disclosed to the Prosecution. And so I am asking leave of the Court because of the late filing of this designation of expert witness to designate Dr. Gripon, and the other expert witnesses that I have on my list, plus an additional motion to designate two additional experts from Holland has been filed, which are a Dr. Ernst Lammers, and a Dr. B. Haeseker, and I don't have the response from the Prosecution regarding that. I believe Ms. McHenry was just aware of this motion this morning. But this is because we are having difficulty getting the doctor in Konjic who performed the surgery on Mr. Landzo, and therefore we have to substitute someone else who can testify about Mr. Landzo's hand injury and his asthma. And that's why we have called Dutch doctors just to go quickly to the prison, examine him, and then come and testify. We expect their testimony to be about one half day each or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: How many experts do you need to examine?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, unfortunately, I don't have my list here with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: How many experts do you intend to examine to refute the eyewitness account?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: To refute the eyewitness account, I have three mental health experts, Dr. Legazzi who has already examined Mr. Landzo as an order of the Court in 1996. I have Dr. Leewuwen who examined Mr. Landzo for his compatibility with detention and competency to stand trial in 1996. Both of those experts will do one additional evaluation and supplement their original reports and the Prosecution has both of those reports. I also have Dr. Edward Gripon, who is a forensic psychiatrist, who also will be completing his evaluation this week. Three mental health experts, one historian and two Dutch doctors about his physical injuries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, what worries me is your attitude towards a report. Now, if you refer to the order of the Trial Chamber of the 25th of January.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I remember. I don't have it in front of me, but I believe the Court ordered that any reports that I had, I had to make available to the Prosecution. I don't have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: And you have not called for any reports?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am calling for a report when he completes his evaluation. Until he is completed, I can't ask him to write a report. He will finish this Friday with his evaluation of Mr. Landzo. At that point, if he writes a report, I will give it directly to the Prosecution. She has all other reports that I have in my possession. I don't believe that under the rules of procedure or the rules of evidence in this Court, I have seen any rule that makes it mandatory for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Well you can disobey that. You can disobey the order because no rules have made it mandatory.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if I have the report made, I will give it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Not making it mandatory. But that's why I say you are free to disobey and not send any reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am not sure that I understand disobey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. Because if there are no compulsory rules and the Trial Chamber makes an order, as you have said, you're entitled to disobey that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am not trying to disobey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: -- the order that you are required to submit any reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, my interpretation of the order was to turn over all reports in my possession. If I have a report in my possession, I will certainly give it to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Then you say so. That you don't have any reports in your possession. That's a short way of telling them that I haven't the reports you're asking for.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I have given them the reports of Dr. Leewuwen and Dr. Lagazzi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Those are even experts nominated by the Trial Chamber itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have given them all supporting data too of Dr. Loga, Dr. Rorta Deman (phoen), Dr. Somalevic (phoen) and any other reports that these experts relied upon, I have disclosed to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose that is what you should say. But not challenging the order of the Trial Chamber that no rules supports the order of the Trial Chamber, then you should know what to do as Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am not challenging the order of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That's what Counsel should normally do. If you are convinced that the order is not supported by any rule of Court or any statutes, you're not obliged to obey and you know what to do in that circumstance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: So you file the reports and then you see what you can do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I have filed them. They have them in their possession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You said Dr. Gripon is still to file his report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: He just arrived last night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: File his report and then see.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You mean he won't be designated until after he files his report. I just want to bring to the Court's attention that two Prosecution witnesses, expert witnesses, testified without reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Maybe after he files his report you find he has nothing to say on the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that could be. After he reports to me on Friday, I might say, "Don't write a report and go home." I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Don't ask us to make an order at this stage when you haven't got a report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I understand now. Thank you very much for explaining it to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That's really unfair matters on what you would be producing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: So the other experts that have provided reports, I assume that there's not going to be any objection from the Prosecution on designation of those experts. And as soon as Dr. Gripon has completed his evaluation and supplied a report, we will bring this issue up again for designation of expert. Now I am clear on that and I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms. McHenry, what's your position?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Certainly we have no opposition to Your Honour's waiting to decide on Dr. Gripon until we've seen the report. I won't speak to that. I do want to just briefly speak to sort of the other, as I understand it, approximately eight expert witnesses that the Defence is going to call. And I will also clarify what Ms. McMurrey said is that in addition to the expert witnesses she just mentioned, I have been informed that there are a number of doctors who were on the expert witness list, I believe two or three, who she still intends to call, but she states that they will be called as fact witnesses rather than as expert witnesses. I am not exactly sure how these doctors can testify about facts without giving their medical opinion and so we may well be objecting to those persons testifying as fact witnesses. With respect to the mental health witnesses, in addition to Dr. Gripon there are two other doctors, and the Prosecution does not object to her calling them. Although this is first we've heard that she is going to have them do additional evaluations and, therefore, presumably, have additional information and do additional reports. Once again, this gets into the entire idea of how can the Prosecution sort of be prepared to effectively cross-examine and do our own research and potentially get our own experts when at, you know, this extensive time already into the Defence case we're still being notified of additional experts and additional witnesses. In addition to the expert witnesses, the Defence has now indicated that they wish to call two additional witnesses as to physical impairment. And again, as the Prosecution stated in its response, we don't even know what, in effect, this Defence is. Your Honour's order very clearly states that the Defence has to give a statement as to what the expert is going to testify to. Given the specialised nature of medical testimony, we do not believe that a three word sentence saying their expert will testify about Mr. Landzo's hand and his opinion about that or his respiratory problems provides the Prosecution or even the Chamber sufficient information to know whether or not this testimony is relevant. And certainly does not allow the Prosecution to prepare. We want to make sure that we are not in a position that after the testimony of an expert witness, we do not want to have to be in a position of asking for some sort of recess while we then do our own research or get our own expert before we can effectively cross-examine. So we have raised these issues at an early date so that when these experts are called, if they are called, things can happen expeditiously. But we believe that the Defence has not complied with Your Honour's order about giving a statement about the subject of the testimony. Similarly, I will just again, there's also a historian who is going to talk about psychology. And again, with respect the that, the Prosecution noted that the Defence has stated that they are going to call a historian. Their only description of what this witness is going to testify about is, "He will testify about the psychology of the ethnic groups and individuals caught up on the war and international humanitarian law." Again, the Prosecution feels this is not in compliance with Your Honour's rule. And certainly, the Prosecution believes that we must have more information to know whether or not we wish to file a motion excluding it as irrelevant or as the expert being unqualified to testify. Or, if it is something relevant and it is something within the expert's expertise, we are going to have to be able to do some research beforehand. So, in all respects with respect to all their expert witnesses, the Prosecution believes the Defence has not complied with this Court's order and it will result in this proceedings being unnecessarily delayed, inefficient and really unjust to the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might respond just for a moment. The request for designation of the Dutch doctors, in my opinion, satisfies the Court's order as far as giving them a statement at the intended testimony. It's clear, number one, Dr. Lammers; not only he is a Dutch pulmonary specialist, who has examined and conducted tests regarding Mr. Landzo, he will offer evidence regarding the type of illness and extent of damage to the lungs. He will further be asked to state his opinion regarding the ability of Mr. Landzo to perform the acts alleged in the indictment. I don't know how many clearer I can be. And Dr. Haeseker, his explanation is just as clear. And if the Court will please kindly compare this explanation to the one paragraph explanation that the Prosecutor gave all Defence attorneys when Professor Economides came to testify, this is much clearer and much more specific. And of course Dr. Economides and Dr. Gal both testified without any report supplied to the Defence at that time. And I believe that I have done -- the Defence of Esad Landzo has worked hard to comply with the orders of the Court at this point. Coming from behind the eight ball as we say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Your defence is going to be that considering his state of physical health, the acts attributed to him could not have possibly have been committed. Is that your defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: That's is really, basically, part of a defence, yes, Your Honour. It's not that all acts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Therefore, you filed the reports of the experts?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, Ms. Boler just whispered in my ear that these doctors will have their reports this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We will consider your motions after we get to the peoples' reports and Ms. McHenry has examined them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might, I am Nancy Boler. I would to just like to add one thing. Dr. Lammers is going on holiday on June 16th. He told me we would have his report before he left. The other doctor, the hand specialist Dr. Haeseker, is currently on holiday and he's going to be gone another week and a half or so. And as soon as he returns, I'll have him get on that right away. When Ms. McMurrey said "this week," I just needed to correct that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Now the Defence is becoming clear, that these acts could not have possibly been committed and you want to examine the expert in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It's not a play for diminished liability , it's a play of impossibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Some of the acts it would be an impossibility and some of the acts it would a diminished possibility. So there are so many different allegations under the Prosecutor's indictment that it would be different level for different acts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Let's have these reports first.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a question regarding that because I am not clear and so that I don't have a mistake before I stand up again in this Court, is it my understanding that the Court will not designate an expert without a written report first?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Expert is fair enough, but relevancy is another matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: So he can be designated as an expert via his curriculum vitae attached, but the relevancy of his testimony needs to be determined by the Court from his report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Naturally. Obviously they are not going to talk about eyewitness accounts. They are going to give their opinion with regard to certain matters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: They are to give their report with respect to certain matters based on their opinion. So let's see what they have to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: So every expert --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Calling these expert witnesses is going to cost the Tribunal a lot of money. We want to be sure that their evidence is relevant. Obviously, I mean there's no dispute that you're calling them as experts. You're not calling them as fact witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Let's have a look at these reports which they have prepared.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Is it my understanding, they have to prepare a report before they're allowed to testify?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: They should file a report because before you ask us to call them here, they're no doubt experts. But they are to come here and we want to be sure of the relevancy of their evidence. That is all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I just wanted, for the record, to state that the Prosecution didn't have reports for two of their experts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: This is what I wanted to correct when you continue repeating that statement. Before the order of 25th January 1997 was made, a lot of arguments was made as to the desirability of having a report. Now, the real reason is to ensure that the expert is coming to say what he knew about the area of expertise and that that area is relevant to the situation in which he has been invited to testify, his evidence. Now when somebody is called to testify about nationality, I don't think any reasonable lawyer knows what nationality is. When he's coming to give you expert testimony on the nationality of the people, all it wanted you to know is that the nationality involved in the situation in which these people found themselves, not for Dr. Gal. It was very familiar. Nobody even asked for a report and nobody even needed it because we knew what he was coming to testify about. So when you continue comparing situations, I began to wonder whether that is the way legal practice is done. Because every lawyer deals with a fact situation facing him. And you don't bring comparisons which in most cases you know are not on the same basis. And you better forget it and face the situation in which you find yourself and argue towards rationality. Now if you bring the present expertise you want to call now, the matter of physical impossibility or reduced physical possibility, this is what you are trying to show. Now, I suppose it's a fairly strange type of argument. Your client doesn't say he's lame. He doesn't say that he has a weak hand. Most asthmatics do so many physical things, what you are now trying to put forward, the Defence you are putting forward is that your client who has short breath cannot do certain things in certain situations. We're not too sure what type of medical expertise is related to it. We should need to know what this doctor is likely to come to testify. I didn't think it was anything unreasonable for a Trial Chamber to ask and to pass on to the Prosecution. If the doubt is that this is -- obviously he is not a fact witness because when it comes to whatever physically he inflicted on people, there are fact witnesses who to come to say they saw him do it. What your expert witness is coming to say that he is incapable of doing this. Or perhaps he cannot do it with such a ferocity. These are the things you're trying to say. In that regard, the expert people need something to guide them if they have to challenge the matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I just have to say that, you know, before the Court has heard the defence, you've already stated it is a strange defence and I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I don't believe it is a strange defence, I think it's a valid defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You file the reports and we'll have a look at it. And as your learned colleague has said, she's expecting the reports within two weeks. So let the reports be filed and then look at the motions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Your Defence will be given full consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Makes one to look into it very critically and be satisfied that it is possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: My only argument at this point, not arguing with the Court at all, is that, as far as the equality of arms goes, the Prosecution -- the Court now understands why I am calling these witnesses as much as they understood why the Prosecution was calling Economides. So, therefore, in the equality of arms issue, I don't believe that I have to offer any more in order for him to be able to testify. It's clear that his testimony is relevant, but to satisfy the Court, I will give any documents that I can at this point and I will provide the reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We gave you long adjournment to get yourself prepared for cross-examination. We don't want this to happen now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I don't want it to happen either, Your Honour. I am ready to go home too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You're the manager of your own case. Nobody stops you. But we're also entitled to know why the case has been so managed. We're entitled to know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I will do my best to make sure that the Court knows why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Perhaps Counsel, is as you mean that, the Trial Chamber is not interested in the case of the accused persons. That would be very, very wrong to think. Because a Court is not interested in finding guilt as much as it is interested in finding innocence. All the facts should be placed before it for it to decide what the true position is. So if it is necessary, the rules are very clear, enabling the Court itself to call witnesses if it finds it necessary in the interest of a Defence or even of the Prosecution. It's entitled to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I have certainly have never thought that the Court wanted anything other than justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I have heard too much about the equality. It's like most Defence counsel, it's only equal when it suits their way. No, but that is not equality. Equality is putting the scales on an even keel.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I thank you. I think that's all I have until I get these reports for the Court. And I hope that the Court will consider all of these expert witnesses that I have listed necessary for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Certainly after you file the report. Certainly, we'll consider you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think this is all we have.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have -- I'm sorry, there's another matter before the Court that I had asked for oral argument on, but I spoke to Ms. McHenry this morning and she said she is not prepared to respond to it and she would like more time. That is Esad Landzo's submissions regarding diminished or lack of mental capacity. It's most important that for the Defence we get some kind of definition on this as soon as possible because we can't determine what burden we have or what standards we have to meet in the Defence case until this is resolved. I told Ms. McHenry this morning, but I certainly agree to allow them more time. I understand it's a difficult legal issue to deal with. I would ask the Court that maybe before we start on June the 22nd, if we could determine this issue, I would be better prepared for the first week in July to make sure that I am ready to present evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The question of the diminished responsibility depends on, perhaps, the state of mind or the medical aptitude, which, perhaps, expert witnesses might have disclosed in their examination. It's only part of the Defence case, except if the Prosecution wants to use it. It's part of the Defence case for the purposes of determining the extent of liability or responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: My question, Your Honour, is that until we know what the definition is that we're dealing with, whether the burden of proof shifts to the Defence and whether the standard of proof at that point is by preponderance of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The burden is obviously on the person who takes it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: -- jurisdictions, that we need to know which one this Court will adopt before we go forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms. McMurrey, all through the trial the burden of proving guilt stays on the Prosecution until the end. If you plead diminished responsibility and you prove that, it does not go towards innocence. It merely shows that your responsibility for committing the act is diminishing to the extent to which you have proved the extent of his mental responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Whether his affirmative Defence negates one of the elements that the Prosecution has to prove.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You can take the quantities of circumstances appearing in the Prosecution's evidence itself to show that it is a case of diminished liability. You have a right to depend upon circumstances appearing from the evidence of the Prosecution itself. Otherwise, the burden is on you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Stays on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Or diminished liability. But you can take it upon them in discharging the burden upon the facts or circumstances appearing from the evidence of the Prosecution itself. You have that advantage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It does not go to acquit, that's one thing you will know. Diminished responsibility doesn't go to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: It lists it in the statute as a defence which means it's not simply mitigation of punishment in this Tribunal. It's a defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The burden is always on the Prosecution. But if you want to take a plea of diminished liability, you can of course take advantage of the evidence of the Prosecution itself in that regard, but the burden of proof is on you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: My one further question on that, the burden of proof shifts to me to prove that he has diminished mental capacity. But what is the standard of proof at that point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: All you have to do is create a reasonable doubt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: By probabilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: To raise a reasonable doubt, this might have happened.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I cited British law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am citing the British law because that's the law in which we were trained.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: It says that when the burden shifts to the Defence -- thank you. I just wanted to make sure that it was a civil burden. I didn't have to prove beyond a reasonable doubt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, it's clear to me now. And if the Prosecution would still like to respond, I think I have heard from the Court what I need to form my Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you want clarity or equality as you're asking of every issue, then it should also prove your reasonable doubt because that's --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: It's not equality of arms under that circumstance, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Here it is a civil body.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you for listening to me because I just needed that definition to proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, you have suggested that the discussion on our motion on June 2nd be postponed. But from our conversation with Ms. McHenry, we understood that maybe there's a response to our motion already. And if we ask that during the break we could see the decision and so that we have time to discuss it amongst ourselves. And also this morning, you have issued a request for subpoena, so that they could be here on the 11th of June so that we could be able to see them here as witnesses. If the chamber would accept our proposals, maybe after the break we could return to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, I am seeing this for the first time now. So I don't really know what it contains.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's why we suggested for a pause and then we could state our opinion on the 2nd of June document. But I believe we could have our opinion on it after the break. And then during the break, you would also have time to see our motion submitted this morning, so that maybe we'd have an opportunity to discuss it during the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we'll be able to have a break now and come back at twelve.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Now, the Trial Chamber has considered the ruling, considered the motion from Delalic for the issue of subpoenas in respect of two of its witnesses against the 11th of June. We've considered the case as a whole, the application, which is not in isolation with what has been going on in the Defence case, and we think that the application has come too late, because when we made that Ruling in respect of the lists submitted to the Trial Chamber, which was phrased in two ways: The first is 1 to 7, the next 8 to 14, and indicating that the lists of witnesses 8 to 14 are unable to appear until the 22nd. We directed Counsel to assure that all the witnesses were called by the end of this week. We made that order. And there was ample time to have applied for any subpoenas at that time. And we indicated in that oral ruling, which we confirmed in our ruling yesterday, that at the conclusion of the last witness Counsel should decide to close the case of the first accused. We made that very clear. Now, it was during this period that Counsel appealed against that ruling and had all opportunities for asking for subpoenas, which was inevitable at that time, knowing that it was necessary for Counsel to get its witnesses here. But they did not do so. Counsel had waited until yesterday, and then the application took for a subpoena was submitted this morning. The Trial Chamber finds it difficult to conceive how the application for subpoena, which is made today, is intended for witnesses outside the jurisdiction and for evidence within the week. In any event, what one was considering is for Counsel to close its case and not to lead new evidence. And for the reasons the Trial Chamber has given, we did not think it was reasonable to grant the application. The application is refused. We still have before us the motion requesting procedures of final determination of charges against the first accused. The Prosecution has reacted to that and the Trial Chamber will be able to hear argument on that motion. That is a motion pending. This is our ruling.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I regret the fact that you have decided the previous motion without our having presented the arguments that we were guided by, but since that is the ruling of the Court, we accept it as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: An application for a subpoena -- I know why you are asking for a subpoena. You have given your reasons in there. It doesn't need any further persuasion. It's not opposed and I know it will not be.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But there was a previous procedure followed in other subpoenas where oral arguments were presented, and that is why I said this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It's not necessary. It's not necessary. You've given sufficient reasons why the subpoena should be granted.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, on the 2nd of June, as you know, with the arguments of the Defence, we sought that the procedure regarding our defendant, Mr. Delalic, be continued in keeping with Article 85 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence before this Court. In view of the fact that the Prosecution has finalised a presentation in respect of their case in respect of our client, and after the Appeals Chamber has decided our appeal on the possible continuation of the presentation of the Defence case, we will also be completing the presentation of our case in the Delalic case. We believe that all our argumentation is grounded. In view of the fact, in the meantime, we have received the Prosecutor's response to our application, I should like to, without repeating what we have already said in written form in seeking this particular decision from the Trial Chamber, I should like to present the position of the Defence regarding the reply of the Prosecution, which we received an hour ago. The first argument of the Prosecutor concerning our request is that we are asking again for a separate trial to be conducted, that we are seeking a separate procedure, a separate trial for Mr. Delalic, which request of the Defence was also filed in 1996, and that it was considered with all due form and decided by this Chamber. In connection with a particular argument of the response, I should like to emphasise that we did not ask for a separate trial, although the Defence, if there is a conflict of interest, is entitled to seeking such a separate trial in any stage of the proceedings. But we did not. We have not asked for a separation of trials, because we consider it not to be necessary because all the conditions now exist for the consistent application of Rule number 85. Because the Prosecution has presented its case, the Defence has presented its evidentiary case, and Rule number 82 says that the accused will be entitled, at the joint trials, the same rights which they would have if they were -- as if they were tried separately. So our position is that availing ourselves of these rights, namely, that as if our client was being tried separately, we propose that the Court bring the decisions and the orders as we proposed in our motion. Namely, first of all, that the Prosecutor should be called upon to present evidence, rebuttal evidence, if any, and then that we are invited to respond and to present any rejoinder evidence, if we have it, and then the Chamber, if it feels that it should present some evidence, also do that. And after that, call upon the parties to present their final arguments. And then, in keeping with the rules of this Tribunal, to proceed to a final decision, in respect of Mr. Delalic. Owing to these reasons, we feel that the response given to our motion by the Prosecutor does not stand, because this motion has nothing whatsoever to do with a possible request for separate trials, because the procedure of the presentation of evidence on the part of both the Prosecution and the Defence has been completed, is being completed at this particular point in time. The following argument, which is given in the Prosecutor's response, is that this would mean an unnecessary delay and duplication of the presentation of the cases in the further course of the proceedings. As opposed to this position of the Prosecution, it is our view that this cannot constitute a duplication or a procrastination of the proceedings, and that Mr. Delalic is entitled to that fundamental right of a speedy and fair trial. If our motion were to be granted, we feel that we would precisely in such a case be economising in terms of the further course of the proceedings, because we would confine the interrogation of every witness by the cross-examination, and we would save the expenses of two attorneys to this court. And the proceedings in general would not be procrastinated because Rule number 85 has to be applied, irrespective of whether it is applied now, in the month of June, or whether it has to be applied by the Court later, after all the cases have been presented. So this stage of the proceedings has to be gone through, and we feel that it is only fair, in respect of Mr. Delalic, that this rule be invoked and applied at this particular stage, especially the one granted by the Rule 82 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. In his response the Prosecutor stresses that this request of ours, actually, prevents the Court from hearing additional relevant evidence. I believe this argumentation to be ungrounded. The Prosecutor had its case, presented all the documents which he considered relevant in order -- in respect of our client. We are not preventing the Prosecutor if he has other evidence. In fact, on the contrary, we are offering to him, if he has other relevant evidence in respect of Mr. Delalic, to present it immediately. We also feel that we have not violated the rights of any of the co-accused because, just as we ourselves had the right to cross-examine all the witnesses presented by the Prosecutor in respect of Mr. Delalic, not only in respect of Mr. Delalic, but also in respect of all the other accused, all the other co-accused have also had the opportunity for a cross-examination of the witnesses and to follow the evidence presented by Mr. Delalic's Counsel during his defence. The Prosecutor is now offering us, although he does not directly say so in his reply, he says that -- the interpreter does not have the document. We wish to prevent the Court from the presentation of evidence of the other accused and thereby to judge possibly the evidence given in respect of Mr. Delalic. It is our position that a fair trial observing the provisions of Article 22 -- 82 in connection with Article 20 of the Statute, must be interpreted so that the Prosecutor does not have the right, that after all the defence has been presented, that other evidence be obtained through the presentation of the cases of the other accused, so that all the evidentiary material has to be presented. The Prosecutor has in the process had the occasion to cross-examine all other -- all our witnesses, and I should like to warn the Prosecutor of the provisions of Article 51 of the rules -- the Rule 51, which is the proper way to deal with this matter, because otherwise Mr. Delalic's right from Rules 82 and 85 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence are denied him. We are conducting this proceeding before a Trial Chamber composed of professional Judges, and not before a jury. Therefore, the argumentation adduced by the Prosecutor to the effect that perhaps the evaluation of evidence in respect of Delalic could create certain prejudice in respect of the evaluation of the evidence against the other accused, in our view does not stand because this Chamber is perfectly capable of evaluating every piece of evidence in respect of every accused, and we believe that there can be no problems along those lines at all. The Defence also relies in its motion to Rule B of Rule 87, which reads that the Trial Chamber of first instance shall deliberate and make decisions for every accused as referred to in the indictment. So at the moment when the Court -- if the Court were to deliberate on all the accused, it would have to evaluate separately every piece of evidence in respect of every accused, each accused, in respect of each count of the indictment. So if the Chamber were to do that at this moment, it would be actually exercising its right and carrying out, in fact, its duty to act in that way, without being able, thereby, to violate that right of the other accused, or prejudicing in any way or prejudging their decision in respect of the other accused. As we have stressed in our written motion, in this way we are practically not undermining any of the co-accused, but we ourselves are actually renouncing certain benefits that we might have from the cross-examination of the other defences that would be offered by other Counsel. And, finally, the Prosecutor emphasises that this example, if it were to be accepted, could be something that would be emulated by other accused persons, and that they would -- could call for a similar decision to be brought after the presentation of their cases. We believe that that is a right to which every accused person is entitled, and each accused and his Defence Counsel have the right to avail themselves of whatever has been envisaged under Article 82 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Finally, we should like also to stress the following, Your Honours. By brief analysis of the proceedings which have been conducted so far, and of, so-to-speak, a new policy being followed by the Prosecutor in this Chamber, namely, that we should not have proceedings with a number of persons, that we should appraise the individual responsibility of each person, because that is much more efficient and much fairer in respect of every accused individual. We have dealt with some data for -- we have examined, rather, some data, and that data says that Mr. Delalic has been in custody for over -- for some two years, and that it is important that his case be decided as soon as possible, especially in view of the fact, if we have the -- both cases already presented. So along those lines we sought to call a maximum and to present our case as briefly and as efficiently as possible over a short period of time, and to deal with every possible element of his defence. To adduce a few examples, for instance, over the first four months and four days, which the Prosecutor had at his disposal during at the beginning of the conduct, he had 44 court days, and over this period of 44 Court days, 25 witnesses were heard. We, on our part, over a period of two months and ten days, namely, 26 Court days, called and heard 25 witnesses in that period. We had a normal interruption of 21 days, a normal recess, but I should like to stress that our own attitude towards the speed with which the cases are presented, the evidence presented, and the instructions by the Court that we are to economise with time, we really treated that with the maximum of responsibility and managed in a record time, as it were, to organise our defence well. And, therefore, we consider that all this entitles us to seeking from this Chamber, in keeping with Rule number 85, to grant us that this motion of ours in respect of our client. These would be our additional arguments, as our reply to the position of the Prosecutor vis-à-vis the positions in the motion filed by the defence of Mr. Delalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This application I have before me, you had earlier asked in 1996 that there should be separate trials. That application was rejected. Isn't this application a continuation of your earlier motion which was rejected?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. In our application we actually rely upon -- invoke Rule 82 where at joint trials the accused will have the rights which they would have if they had separate trials. Then we also invoke Rule 87, where it says that the first instance Trial Chamber will vote separately for every accusation given in the indictment. And if there is a number of indictees, separate sentences will be handed down and/or -- so Rule 83, which says after the presentation of evidence of both sides, the Prosecution will be invited to give its evidence in rebuttal and, therefore, the Defence in its own rejoinder. So Rules 82, 85, namely, that the person who is in a joint trial has the same right as the person being tried individually, gives us the right to ask that after the Prosecutor has presented its case, and we have presented our case, that the case be finalised in respect of our client. We are not asking for a separate trial. The cases have been presented. We are asking for the finalisation, for the completion of the trial in respect of Mr. Delalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any reaction on the part of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Your Honours, the application by the Defence, and I am responding to the submissions just made by Ms. Residovic, and then I'll come back and make some general points, if I may. But the application that she explains to us now is really an application for severance, or separate trial, dressed up and presented in another way. It's no more than that. You can't say that that part of the case, which relates to the presentation of the evidence of the Prosecution and the Defence is the trial, and then leave out those other parts of the case, namely, the rebuttal, rejoinder submission and sentence, and say that that's some other creature. Your Honours, it's part and parcel of the same species. It's all the trial. So, in my submission, Your Honour, it is to no avail for Madam Residovic to argue that she has now presented to you something novel and different from that with which you've already disposed of and dealt with. Your Honours, there is no right for separate trial. There is no such right. And there is no right, under Rule 85, for these events, when you do have a joint trial, for the events, such as rebuttal, rejoinder, sentence, submissions, and so forth, to follow immediately after the other in relation to each separate accused. There is no such right. It doesn't exist. So the support and basis for that would be something I would be most interested to see. These matters follow in the sequence of the trial, and if there is a joint trial, then the Prosecutor can present the evidence jointly in relation to all accused, and has done so, and can likewise respond in rebuttal and in submissions. Your Honours, just a couple of general points. Firstly, in our submission, I restate that Your Honours have ruled they have presented nothing different, or nothing new, to say while Your Honours should reconsider your previous decision, and on that basis alone, Your Honours, we submit that Your Honours shouldn't entertain the application. The interests of the public and the Prosecution, in having a separate trial, is something which is different to what happens in a number of instances when it comes to considerations and fair trials. The reason for that is that, generally speaking, the authority, at least in some -- in most jurisdictions, leans towards a conclusion, that the interests of the public and the Prosecution, in having separate trials -- in having a joint trial outweighs the interests of the Defence in having a separate trial. And so the next principle for consideration, it's generally a question of prejudice, and it's not just ordinary prejudice. The mere fact that the accused can point to some prejudice is not sufficient. For example, in the case of the United Kingdom, the prejudice there that has to be demonstrated is dangerous prejudice. In relation to our own Tribunal, Rule 82 uses the words "serious prejudice." 82B, it refers to serious prejudice. So, Your Honours, the -- in this one and somewhat unusual incident, the right of the public, and the Prosecution, to have joint trials generally outweighs the interests of the accused, separate accused, unless you get to that point of either serious or dangerous prejudice. And neither of that, in any way, has been demonstrated. Indeed, the converse is the case. We have seen with these accused there's been very little evidence whatsoever of conflicts emerging between them throughout the course of this trial. What happens in the back rooms, we don't know, but what we've seen in the courtroom is sufficient, in my respectful submission, to allay any concerns that Your Honours may have in relation to that matter. Your Honours, this is an application for a separate trial, which will not only lead to a separate trial for the rest of these proceedings being separate trials for the accused, Delalic. There is absolutely nothing that they can point to to demonstrate that Mr. Delalic is in any different position to any of the other accused. So Your Honours will be confronted with a situation where you will have now bifurcated proceedings in relation to all accused because, I submit, Your Honours will be able to find no distinction between them. And so that we will have rebuttal evidence on four occasions. We'll have closing addresses on four. We'll have sentencing evidence on four occasions. We'll have sentencing on four occasions. I can assure Your Honours that if we go down this route, these proceedings will be protracted for a very, very long time. In our submission, Your Honours, that on the basis of all of that, this application should be rejected. If I can assist Your Honours with any more, that's my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we've heard the arguments, except if you have anything to add.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We just wanted to say the following. We do not look for severance of trials in the sense of the Article 82, paragraph 2. We are speaking of 81, paragraph 1. And the prosecutor said that there's no rule which would enable us to do so. I have stated several and I do not see one which would prevent this Trial Chamber from accepting our proposal. In such a situation, I believe the ruling should be for the better of the Defence or the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We've heard your arguments. We'll give our ruling later. We'll give our rulings. I expect that perhaps you might reply to the inevitable consequence of granting your application in the nature of multiplying each accused's right to separate addresses, separate closing addresses and all that follows with each of them, rebuttal for each of them. Instead of rebuttal for all of them as a whole right. This is the only argument of interest and I will look at it and see whether it is desirable in the interest of justice as a whole to consider your application. Thank you. So the Trial Chamber will now rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: 12.40 p.m., to the reconvened on the 22nd day of June, 1998, at 10.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
